name: Walking Preference: Street Segments and Intersections (Tokyo)
description:
Method replication: same task, scales and design as the paper; the images are not the paper's stimuli (88 new Google Street View views of Setagaya Ward, Tokyo, 2016–2026: 58 street segments and 30 intersections).

Huang, Oki, Muto & Ogawa (2024, ISPRS IJGI) ran an online pairwise image survey with about 18,000 respondents living in Japan (over 120,000 responses, 10 per pair) to train models of walking preference across Setagaya Ward, then related eye-level streetscape factors to the scores with XGBoost and SHAP. On a phone-style screen participants saw one street view above the other and answered "Which street segment is preferable for walking?" or "Which street intersection is preferable for walking?" on a five-point scale: Upper image is much better than Bottom image / Upper image is somewhat better than Bottom image / Both are the same / Bottom image is somewhat better than Upper image / Bottom image is much better than Upper image.

This template keeps the two questions, the upper/bottom layout and the five levels. Each answer is stored twice: as a pairwise choice with tie (upper, bottom or "Both are the same", ranked with TrueSkill on Results) and, in comparison_levels, as the signed level (+2 … -2) with the upper and bottom image names.

Differences from the original study: (1) images: the paper used front-view GSV images at 30 m intervals along the road network (1,000 segment and 200 intersection images, each paired with others ten times); here 58 segment views from a grid over the ward and 30 intersection views (panoramas where three or more street directions meet, viewed at or just before the junction), paired at random; (2) each participant does 10 segment pairs then 4 intersection pairs (the paper had no fixed number, 6.6 responses per respondent on average); (3) English wording (the original interface was Japanese; the English labels are the paper's translation); (4) optional age and gender questions added to describe the sample (the paper balanced age and gender through the survey company).

Street images: Google Street View (© Google).
author: Huang, Oki, Muto & Ogawa
